questions.text: A fall in the price of good 1 changes demand through which two channels?

options.a: A technology effect and an endowment effect.
options.b: A supply effect and a productivity effect.
options.c: A tax effect and an inflation effect.
options.d: A substitution effect and an income effect.

questions.text: The substitution effect of a price change primarily captures a change in what?

options.a: The relative opportunity cost of goods, holding purchasing power or utility constant.
options.b: The quantity of income earned from selling labor.
options.c: Nominal income with all prices unchanged.
options.d: Consumer preferences following advertising.

questions.text: The income effect of a price change captures what?

options.a: The response of market supply to higher wages.
options.b: The effect of changed purchasing power at the new relative prices.
options.c: A shift in preferences caused by higher income taxes.
options.d: The effect of changing relative prices at fixed purchasing power.

questions.text: In the Slutsky decomposition, the compensated budget line passes through which bundle?

options.a: The consumer's original chosen bundle.
options.b: The point where the new budget line meets the vertical axis.
options.c: The bundle with zero consumption of good 1.
options.d: The consumer's final chosen bundle.

questions.text: For a price change from p1 to p1', what is the Slutsky income compensation?

options.a: The original quantity of good 1 multiplied by the price change, x1 times (p1' - p1).
options.b: The final quantity of good 1 multiplied by original income.
options.c: The original income multiplied by the percentage price change.
options.d: The change in utility multiplied by the price of good 2.

questions.text: When the price of good 1 falls and the price of good 2 stays fixed, the budget line does what?

options.a: Pivots inward around its horizontal intercept.
options.b: Pivots outward around its vertical intercept.
options.c: Becomes steeper while keeping the same horizontal intercept.
options.d: Shifts inward in parallel.

questions.text: Under standard convex preferences, a compensated own-price substitution effect is what?

options.a: Always zero regardless of preferences.
options.b: Nonpositive when the own price rises.
options.c: Always positive when the own price rises.
options.d: Identical to the income effect.

questions.text: For a normal good, what happens when its own price falls?

options.a: The income effect must be zero.
options.b: Both the substitution and income effects increase its demand.
options.c: Substitution decreases demand while income increases it.
options.d: Both effects reduce its demand.

questions.text: For an inferior good, how do the substitution and income effects of an own-price increase compare?

options.a: They are necessarily both positive.
options.b: They must have the same magnitude.
options.c: They are necessarily both negative.
options.d: They act in opposite directions.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes an inferior good from a Giffen good?

options.a: Every inferior good is a Giffen good.
options.b: Every Giffen good is normal at low incomes.
options.c: A Giffen good is inferior with an income effect strong enough to reverse the usual own-price response.
options.d: A Giffen good has a positive substitution effect of an own-price increase.

questions.text: If the price of a Giffen good rises, its Marshallian quantity demanded does what?

options.a: Must stay constant.
options.b: Decreases because substitution always dominates.
options.c: Increases.
options.d: Falls to zero immediately.

questions.text: What must be true for an inferior good to display Giffen behavior following a price rise?

options.a: The consumer's nominal income must increase.
options.b: The substitution effect must be positive.
options.c: The positive income effect on its demand exceeds the negative substitution effect.
options.d: The good must have perfect substitutes.

questions.text: For a normal good, which claim is implied by the law of demand discussed in the slides?

options.a: Increasing its own price, holding nominal income fixed, reduces its demand.
options.b: Its demand never responds to prices.
options.c: Compensated demand rises with its own price.
options.d: Raising its own price must increase its demand.

questions.text: What does the Slutsky identity express?

options.a: Income elasticity equals price elasticity plus expenditure share.
options.b: Utility change equals producer surplus plus tax revenue.
options.c: Total demand change equals substitution effect plus income effect.
options.d: Total demand change equals two income effects.

questions.text: Why is a Slutsky-compensated bundle generally different from the original optimum?

options.a: Preferences must have changed.
options.b: Relative prices have changed even though the old bundle remains affordable.
options.c: The compensated line has exactly the old slope.
options.d: Income has increased by the same amount for all goods.

questions.text: For perfect-complements preferences in fixed proportions, the Slutsky substitution effect of an own-price change is typically what?

options.a: The entire Marshallian quantity response.
options.b: Positive for an own-price increase.
options.c: Equal to the consumer's original income.
options.d: Zero, because the optimal consumption ratio remains fixed.

questions.text: For a quasilinear utility function u(x1,x2) = v(x1) + x2 with an interior optimum, the own-price income effect on x1 is what?

options.a: Strictly positive.
options.b: Equal to the price change.
options.c: Strictly negative.
options.d: Zero.

questions.text: Under quasilinear preferences with no income effect on good 1, what follows?

options.a: The change in Marshallian demand for good 1 is entirely a substitution effect.
options.b: The substitution effect must vanish.
options.c: Good 1 must be Giffen.
options.d: Compensated demand is vertical.

questions.text: With perfect substitutes and a price change that switches the cheapest good, what kind of demand change may occur?

options.a: A smooth adjustment at a tangency on a strictly convex indifference curve.
options.b: An increase in both goods at unchanged income.
options.c: A discrete switch from one corner bundle to another.
options.d: An unchanged optimal mix at all prices.

questions.text: What remains constant under Hicks compensation?

options.a: Nominal income.
options.b: Both quantities consumed.
options.c: The consumer's utility level.
options.d: The affordability of the initial physical bundle only.

questions.text: What remains constant under Slutsky compensation?

options.a: Utility at exactly its initial level.
options.b: The expenditure on each good separately.
options.c: The purchasing power needed to afford the original bundle.
options.d: The original relative prices.

questions.text: How is a Hicksian demand function defined?

options.a: The cost-minimizing factor input at target output.
options.b: The profit-maximizing quantity produced at given output price.
options.c: The expenditure-minimizing quantity of a good at given prices and target utility.
options.d: The utility-maximizing quantity at given prices and money income.

questions.text: Which arguments determine Hicksian demand for good 1?

options.a: The firm's output price and fixed costs.
options.b: Target profit and labor supply.
options.c: Both goods' prices and money income only.
options.d: Both goods' prices and a target utility level.

questions.text: Which arguments determine Marshallian demand for good 1?

options.a: Utility level and technology alone.
options.b: Output price and marginal costs.
options.c: Prices and a required utility level.
options.d: Prices and money income.

questions.text: What is the consumer's expenditure-minimization problem?

options.a: Maximize utility while choosing prices.
options.b: Minimize spending while attaining at least a specified utility level.
options.c: Minimize utility subject to a budget.
options.d: Maximize spending subject to earning a given income.

questions.text: The expenditure function e(p1,p2,u) reports what?

options.a: Total consumer income before taxes.
options.b: The minimum money needed to attain utility u at the specified prices.
options.c: The sum of market quantities demanded.
options.d: The maximum profit obtainable at utility u.

questions.text: Shephard's lemma in consumer theory states which result?

options.a: The derivative of expenditure with respect to utility gives Marshallian demand.
options.b: The derivative of market demand with respect to income gives the profit function.
options.c: The derivative of utility with respect to income gives Hicksian demand.
options.d: The derivative of the expenditure function with respect to a good's price gives its Hicksian demand.

questions.text: At prices and income where the consumer achieves utility u, what is true of Marshallian and Hicksian quantities?

options.a: They coincide when Hicksian demand is evaluated at that achieved utility.
options.b: They must differ because one is compensated.
options.c: Marshallian quantity equals the negative of Hicksian quantity.
options.d: Hicksian quantity is always greater for every good.

questions.text: Which optimization problems are dual in consumer theory?

options.a: Expected-value maximization and monopoly pricing.
options.b: Labor supply and market demand aggregation.
options.c: Profit maximization and tax-revenue maximization.
options.d: Utility maximization subject to a budget and expenditure minimization subject to utility.

questions.text: For a differentiable interior expenditure optimum, what condition links preferences and prices?

options.a: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
options.b: The marginal utility of each good must equal one.
options.c: Every good has unit income elasticity.
options.d: The marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio.

questions.text: Which term in the differential Slutsky equation captures the income effect on own demand?

options.a: Minus consumption of good 1 times its marginal propensity to consume good 1 out of income.
options.b: The ratio of factor prices.
options.c: A positive substitution term equal to income itself.
options.d: Plus marginal cost times output.

questions.text: The differential Slutsky equation for own-price effects can be written how?

options.a: Hicksian own-price derivative equals negative consumption times its own price.
options.b: Marshallian demand equals Hicksian demand minus the market supply curve.
options.c: Marshallian own-price derivative equals Hicksian own-price derivative minus x1 times the income derivative of Marshallian x1.
options.d: Marshallian own-price derivative equals Hicksian own-price derivative plus income itself.

questions.text: A good with a zero income derivative has which property under the Slutsky equation?

options.a: Its Marshallian demand must slope upward.
options.b: Its income effect exceeds substitution.
options.c: Its Hicksian demand is always zero.
options.d: Its Marshallian and Hicksian own-price derivatives coincide at matching utility and income.

questions.text: If a good is normal, what sign does its income derivative have?

options.a: Positive.
options.b: Exactly zero by definition.
options.c: Negative.
options.d: Necessarily greater than its price derivative.

questions.text: If a good is inferior, what sign does its income derivative have?

options.a: Negative.
options.b: Positive.
options.c: Always exactly one.
options.d: Undefined at every consumption bundle.

questions.text: What is a basic implication of the compensated law of demand?

options.a: Hicksian own-price demand cannot increase as its own price increases, under standard assumptions.
options.b: Hicksian demand is independent of all prices.
options.c: Marshallian demand can never slope upward.
options.d: Hicksian demand must rise with every price increase.

questions.text: If the cross-price Slutsky substitution matrix is symmetric, what equality holds?

options.a: The compensated cross-price effects are symmetric for the two goods.
options.b: The Marshallian cross-price effects always vanish.
options.c: The own-price effects equal the corresponding quantities.
options.d: Income derivatives are identical for all goods.

questions.text: Why can Marshallian demand violate the ordinary own-price law while Hicksian demand does not?

options.a: Hicksian demand accounts for advertising but Marshallian demand does not.
options.b: Hicksian demand holds market supply fixed.
options.c: The two demands are derived from unrelated preferences.
options.d: Income effects may overpower substitution effects in Marshallian demand.

questions.text: In a two-good model, an increase in the price of good 1 with its own quantity rising indicates what?

options.a: The good exhibits Giffen behavior over that price change.
options.b: The good must be luxury.
options.c: Its compensated demand has increased.
options.d: Its income elasticity is positive.

questions.text: What does a movement along the Hicksian demand curve isolate?

options.a: Changes in market supply at fixed wages.
options.b: Demand adjustment to income holding price fixed.
options.c: Demand adjustment to price holding utility fixed.
options.d: Changes in preferences at fixed prices.

questions.text: In the primal utility-maximization problem, which constraint is central?

options.a: A minimum utility target but no budget.
options.b: Fixed marginal cost.
options.c: The budget constraint.
options.d: Constant firm profits.

questions.text: If the price of one good falls, what is the Hicksian substitution incentive for that good?

options.a: To consume weakly less because purchasing power is held fixed.
options.b: To consume weakly more of the relatively cheaper good.
options.c: To reduce total utility by the price reduction.
options.d: To keep its quantity fixed for every preference.

questions.text: What distinguishes a movement from an original bundle to the Slutsky-compensated optimum from the movement to the final optimum?

options.a: Both are unrelated to the price change.
options.b: The first is substitution; the second is the income effect at new prices.
options.c: The first is income; the second is substitution at old prices.
options.d: Both are income effects.

questions.text: The substitution effect for a good that becomes more expensive is described most accurately as what?

options.a: An unambiguous increase in its compensated quantity.
options.b: A weak reduction in its compensated quantity demanded.
options.c: A change in nominal income alone.
options.d: A rise in the good's marginal utility at all bundles.

questions.text: In the illustrated X-Y-Z Slutsky decomposition, which movement is the substitution effect?

options.a: The movement of the vertical intercept only.
options.b: The movement from the original bundle X to compensated bundle Y.
options.c: The movement from Y to final bundle Z.
options.d: The entire movement from X to Z is purely an income effect.
